key_terms.meaning: Signed number of moles of species i produced per mole of reaction; negative for reactants, positive for products
Reaction-progress variable in mol; nᵢ = nᵢ₀ + νᵢξ for every species
The smallest set of reactions that can produce every observed composition change; count R = N − rank(A), where N = number of species and A = the atomic (element) matrix
Total moles n = n₀ + ξ Σνᵢ, so mole fractions yᵢ = (nᵢ₀ + νᵢξ) / (n₀ + ξΣνᵢ)
Partial molar Gibbs energy of species i, μᵢ = (∂G/∂nᵢ) at fixed T, P and other n's; units J/mol
At fixed T and P in a closed system, equilibrium is where total G is minimum, i.e. (∂G/∂ξ) = 0, equivalently Σνᵢμᵢ = 0 (Aᵢ = affinity = 0)
Dimensionless measure of a species relative to its standard state; μᵢ = G°ᵢ + RT ln aᵢ
The reference state at which aᵢ = 1: pure gas at 1 bar behaving ideally, pure liquid or solid at 1 bar, solute at 1 molal or 1 molar as chosen
ΔG° = ΣνᵢG°ᵢ, the reaction Gibbs energy when every species is in its standard state; depends on T only
K = exp(−ΔG°/RT) = Π aᵢ<sup>νᵢ</sup> at equilibrium; a pure number at a given temperature
d(ln K)/dT = ΔH°/(RT²); equivalently d(ln K)/d(1/T) = −ΔH°/R
ΔH° = ΣνᵢH°ᵢ; its sign decides whether K rises (endothermic) or falls (exothermic) with temperature
ln K = −ΔG°/(RT) = −ΔH°/(RT) + ΔS°/R, using standard free energies of formation at the temperature of interest
Q = Π aᵢ<sup>νᵢ</sup> at the actual (non-equilibrium) composition; Q < K means the forward reaction is feasible, Q > K means the reverse
Fraction of the limiting reactant converted at equilibrium; for A → products with ν<sub>A</sub> = −1, X = (n<sub>A</sub>0 − n<sub>A</sub>)/n<sub>A</sub>0
Yield = moles of desired product formed per mole of limiting reactant fed; selectivity = desired product per competing undesired product
For gases K = K<sub>y</sub> K<sub>p</sub><sup>Σν</sup>, with K<sub>y</sub> = Π yᵢ<sup>νᵢ</sup>; raising P shifts equilibrium toward the side with fewer gas moles when Σν < 0
Adding an inert raises total moles, lowers every yᵢ, and pushes equilibrium toward the side with more gas moles
φᵢ = f̂ᵢ /(yᵢP) with f̂ᵢ = yᵢφᵢP; for ideal gases φᵢ = 1 and K becomes K<sub>p</sub> in bars
With R independent reactions, equilibrium needs R equations Σᵢνᵢⱼμᵢ = 0, j = 1…R, plus element balances, solved for ξ₁…ξ<sub>R</sub>

takeaways: A reacting mixture needs only stoichiometric coefficients and one extent variable per independent reaction to fix every mole number.
At fixed T and P a closed reacting system stops changing when total Gibbs energy is minimum, which is the same statement as Σνᵢμᵢ = 0.
The standard Gibbs energy change sets K through ΔG° = −RT ln K, and K itself depends only on temperature, never on pressure or initial composition.
Van't Hoff's equation turns tabulated ΔH° data into K at any other temperature; endothermic reactions are favoured by heating, exothermic ones by cooling.
K is a number, not a composition: converting it to conversions needs activities, mole balances and, for gases, the pressure and inert content.
Q versus K decides feasibility at the current composition; equilibrium conversion and yield say how far the feed can actually go.
Raising pressure helps only reactions that reduce the number of gas moles; inert dilution always works against them and is best removed by purge.
Real problems stack nonideality, several phases and several reactions, so each reaction gets its own equilibrium relation over one shared set of mole balances.
bank_note: Long answers are expected to move from the Gibbs-minimisation criterion to the K expression, then apply van't Hoff, pressure and inert effects, and finish with numerical conversion or multireaction balances.

bank.q: Define the extent of reaction and show that a reacting mixture with N species and R independent reactions needs exactly R extent variables. How is R found from the atomic matrix?
outline: Write nᵢ = nᵢ₀ + Σⱼνᵢⱼξⱼ for R reactions.
State that each ξⱼ is zero at the start, positive when reaction j runs as written and negative when it runs backwards, bounded so that no nᵢ becomes negative.
Build the element-by-species atomic matrix A and note that element balances conserve atoms for every ξ set.
Independent reactions = N − rank(A); explain that dependent reactions add no new composition change.
Give one worked count: steam reforming species CH₄, H₂O, CO, CO₂, H₂ (N = 5) contain C, H, O with rank 3, so R = 2.
answer: Extent. For one reaction written as Σνᵢ Aᵢ = 0, every mole number follows from one variable: nᵢ = nᵢ₀ + νᵢξ. ξ (mol) is the moles of reaction as written that have occurred; it is zero at the start, positive when the reaction runs forward and negative when it runs backwards, and bounded so that no nᵢ becomes negative.
Several reactions. With R independent reactions, nᵢ = nᵢ₀ + Σⱼνᵢⱼξⱼ. The vector of changes nᵢ − nᵢ₀ is a combination of the R reaction vectors νⱼ, so R extents describe every reachable composition.

Why exactly R. Fewer than R extents cannot reach every composition the reactions allow. More than R adds a reaction vector that is a combination of the others: its extent can be absorbed into the others, so it adds no new composition change and makes the extents non-unique.

Atom matrix. Write a matrix with one row per element and one column per species, each entry the number of atoms of that element in that species. Every reaction conserves atoms, so every reaction vector lies in the null space of this matrix. If its rank is rank(A), the null space has dimension N − rank(A), and R = N − rank(A).

answer.text: Worked count: steam reforming. Species CH₄, H₂O, CO, CO₂, H₂ (N = 5).

answer: Result. The three rows are independent, so rank(A) = 3 and R = 5 − 3 = 2. Choose CH₄ + H₂O → CO + 3H₂ and CO + H₂O → CO₂ + H₂; the overall CH₄ + 2H₂O → CO₂ + 4H₂ is their sum and adds no third extent.

bank.q: Derive the equilibrium criterion Σνᵢμᵢ = 0 for a closed system held at fixed temperature and pressure, starting from dG.
outline: Write dG = −S dT + V dP + Σμᵢ dnᵢ.
At fixed T and P the first two terms vanish, leaving dG = Σμᵢ dnᵢ.
Substitute dnᵢ = νᵢ dξ to get dG = (Σνᵢμᵢ) dξ.
At equilibrium G is minimum, so dG/dξ = 0, hence Σνᵢμᵢ = 0; second derivative positive for a stable minimum.
Note the affinity A = −Σνᵢμᵢ drives the reaction and vanishes at equilibrium.
Mention that at fixed T and V the Helmholtz energy is minimised instead; the criterion Σνᵢμᵢ = 0 is the same.
answer: Start. For a single phase, d(nG) = −(nS) dT + (nV) dP + Σμᵢ dnᵢ, where μᵢ = [∂(nG)/∂nᵢ] at fixed T, P and the other moles.
Fixed T and P. With dT = 0 and dP = 0, d(nG) = Σμᵢ dnᵢ. For a closed system at fixed T and P, every spontaneous change lowers nG, so equilibrium is the state of minimum nG.
Introduce the extent. In a closed system the moles change only by reaction: dnᵢ = νᵢ dξ. So d(nG) = (Σνᵢμᵢ) dξ and [∂(nG)/∂ξ]T,P = Σνᵢμᵢ = ΔGr, the reaction Gibbs energy.
Criterion. At the minimum the slope is zero: Σνᵢμᵢ = 0. For stability the curvature is positive, ∂²(nG)/∂ξ² > 0. If Σνᵢμᵢ < 0 the forward reaction lowers G and proceeds; if > 0 the reverse does.

answer.text: Worked illustration (A ⇌ B, ideal gas, 500 K, 1 bar, ΔG° = −4.00 kJ/mol, 1 mol A fed, RT = 4157 J/mol):
answer.pre:
G − μ<sub>A</sub>° = ξΔG° + RT[(1 − ξ)ln(1 − ξ) + ξ ln ξ]
dG/dξ   = ΔG° + RT ln[ξ/(1 − ξ)]
ξ = 0.25: −4000 − 4567 = −8567 J/mol  (forward)
ξ = 0.90: −4000 + 9134 = +5134 J/mol  (reverse)
minimum: ξ/(1 − ξ) = e<sup>0.9622</sup> = 2.617 → ξ = 0.724 mol, G − μ<sub>A</sub>° = −5345 J

answer: Affinity. A = −Σνᵢμᵢ is the driving force; it is positive while the forward reaction can proceed and zero at equilibrium.
Link to K. Writing μᵢ = μᵢ° + RT ln aᵢ turns Σνᵢμᵢ = 0 into ΔG° + RT ln Π aᵢνᵢ = 0, i.e. ΔG° = −RT ln K. In the example K = e0.9622 = 2.617 = yB/yA, consistent with ξ = 0.724.
Other constraints. At fixed T and V the Helmholtz energy is minimised instead; since μᵢ is the same partial derivative, the criterion Σνᵢμᵢ = 0 is unchanged.

bank.q: Define standard state and activity, and derive K = Π aᵢ<sup>νᵢ</sup> from μᵢ = G°ᵢ + RT ln aᵢ.
outline: Define standard state for gas, liquid and solid; aᵢ = 1 there.
Write μᵢ = G°ᵢ + RT ln aᵢ and substitute into Σνᵢμᵢ = 0.
Collect ΣνᵢG°ᵢ = ΔG° and Σνᵢ ln aᵢ = ln Π aᵢ<sup>νᵢ</sup>.
Obtain ΔG° = −RT ln K with K = Π aᵢ<sup>νᵢ</sup> at equilibrium.
Point out K is dimensionless and depends on T only, not on P or feed.
answer: Standard state. A chosen reference condition of each species at the system temperature: for a gas, the pure ideal gas at P° = 1 bar; for a liquid, the pure liquid at T (and 1 bar or the system pressure); for a solid, the pure solid. The standard chemical potential is G°ᵢ = μᵢ°.
Activity. Defined by μᵢ = G°ᵢ + RT ln aᵢ, so aᵢ = f̂ᵢ/fᵢ°. In the standard state aᵢ = 1. Gas: aᵢ = φ̂ᵢyᵢP/P°. Liquid: aᵢ = γᵢxᵢ. Pure solid or liquid: aᵢ = 1.
Substitute into the criterion. Σνᵢμᵢ = 0 becomes ΣνᵢG°ᵢ + RT Σνᵢ ln aᵢ = 0.
Collect terms. ΣνᵢG°ᵢ = ΔG°, the standard Gibbs energy change, and Σνᵢ ln aᵢ = ln Π aᵢνᵢ. Hence ΔG° = −RT ln Π aᵢνᵢ.
Define K. K = Π aᵢνᵢ (at equilibrium) = exp(−ΔG°/RT). ΔG° depends only on T (for fixed standard states), so K depends only on T, not on pressure or the feed.

answer.text: Worked numbers: ammonia at 298.15 K (ΔGf°(NH₃, g) = −16.45 kJ/mol):

answer: Dimensionless K. Each activity is a ratio (f̂ᵢ/P°, or γᵢxᵢ), so K has no units. A Kp built from partial pressures in bar equals K only because P° = 1 bar; in other units it carries (P°)Σν.
Consistency. Changing a standard state changes G°ᵢ and therefore ΔG° and K, but the matching activities change too, so the predicted equilibrium composition is the same.

bank.q: For N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃, K = 5.81 × 10⁵ at 298.15 K and ΔH°₂₉₈ = −92.22 kJ/mol. Using van't Hoff's equation, obtain K at 500 K for (a) constant ΔH° and (b) ΔH° varying linearly with temperature, taking ΔCp° = −38.3 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ as constant.
outline: Start from d(ln K)/dT = ΔH°/(RT²).
Case (a): integrate to ln(K₂/K₁) = −(ΔH°/R)(1/T₂ − 1/T₁).
Substitute numbers with ΔH° in J/mol and T in kelvin; state the sign convention for exothermic reactions.
Case (b): write ΔH°(T) = ΔH°₀ + ΔC°p (T − T₀) and integrate term by term.
Comment that K falls with rising T when ΔH° < 0 and rises when ΔH° > 0.
Warn that the integrated form is exact only for the assumed ΔH° behaviour.
answer: Equation. d ln K/dT = ΔH°/(RT²), from d(ΔG°/RT)/dT = −ΔH°/(RT²).
(a) Constant ΔH°. Integrate: ln(K₂/K₁) = −(ΔH°/R)(1/T₂ − 1/T₁).
(b) ΔH° linear in T. With constant ΔCp°, ΔH°(T) = ΔH₀° + ΔCp°(T − T₀). Substituting and integrating from T₀ to T: ln(K/K₀) = −[(ΔH₀° − ΔCp°T₀)/R](1/T − 1/T₀) + (ΔCp°/R) ln(T/T₀).

Comparison. Case (b) gives 0.103 against 0.174 for case (a), close to the 0.100 from the full temperature-dependent heat capacities. ΔH° itself grows to −92.22 − 38.3 × 0.2019 = −99.96 kJ/mol at 500 K, so the reaction is more exothermic there and K falls faster.
Sign rule. ΔH° < 0: K falls as T rises (here by a factor of about 6 × 10⁶ between 298 and 500 K). ΔH° > 0: K rises with T. This is Le Chatelier's principle with heat as a product or reactant.
Limits. The constant-ΔH° form is exact only if ΔCp° = 0, and case (b) only if ΔCp° is constant; over hundreds of kelvin use Cp(T) polynomials or integrate numerically.

bank.q: For N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ with a stoichiometric feed at 700 K and 200 bar, write the equilibrium relation in terms of the conversion of N₂ and calculate the equilibrium conversion for K = 8.56 × 10⁻⁵, taking ideal gases.
outline: Take basis 1 mol N₂ + 3 mol H₂, ξ = X with X the fractional conversion of N₂.
Moles: N₂ = 1 − X, H₂ = 3 − 3X, NH₃ = 2X, total = 4 − 2X.
Mole fractions from the total; note Σν = −2.
Write K = [y<sub>NH₃</sub>²/(y<sub>N₂</sub> y<sub>H₂</sub>³)](P/P°)<sup>−2</sup>.
Insert yᵢ(X) to get one algebraic equation in X; solve numerically and keep the root in 0 ≤ X < 1.
State the result as a conversion with units of mol N₂ converted per mol fed.
answer: Basis. 1 mol N₂ + 3 mol H₂; let X be the conversion of N₂, which equals the extent in mol.
Moles. N₂ = 1 − X, H₂ = 3(1 − X), NH₃ = 2X, total = 4 − 2X. Σν = 2 − 1 − 3 = −2.
Mole fractions. yN₂ = (1 − X)/(4 − 2X), yH₂ = 3(1 − X)/(4 − 2X), yNH₃ = 2X/(4 − 2X).
Equilibrium relation (ideal gas, P° = 1 bar): K = [yNH₃²/(yN₂ yH₂³)](P/P°)⁻². Substituting, yNH₃²/(yN₂ yH₂³) = 4X²(4 − 2X)²/[27(1 − X)⁴] = 16X²(2 − X)²/[27(1 − X)⁴].
Result. X = 0.458: 45.8 % of the N₂ is converted; the gas holds yNH₃ = 0.916/3.084 = 0.297, yN₂ = 0.176, yH₂ = 0.527.

Comments. Keep the root with 0 ≤ X < 1. At 200 bar the real gases are non-ideal (φᵢ ≠ 1), so a design calculation multiplies the left side by Kφ = φNH₃²/(φN₂φH₂³). The low K at 700 K (exothermic reaction) is offset by the high pressure, which is why synthesis loops run at 150–300 bar.

bank.q: Explain and illustrate how total pressure and inert addition change the equilibrium conversion of a gas reaction whose Σν is negative, keeping temperature fixed. Use ammonia synthesis at 500 K (K = 0.100) with a stoichiometric feed at 1 and 100 bar, and with 10 mol % argon at 100 bar.
outline: K is fixed at fixed T; only K<sub>y</sub> can change with P and inerts.
K = K<sub>y</sub> (P/P°)<sup>Σν</sup>, so K<sub>y</sub> = K (P/P°)<sup>−Σν</sup>.
For Σν < 0, raising P raises K<sub>y</sub> and hence conversion.
Adding inerts lowers all yᵢ, lowers K<sub>y</sub>, and shifts equilibrium backward for Σν < 0.
Show the yᵢ expressions with the inert mole number in the total.
Industrial note: purge inert gas to protect conversion; high pressure is used in ammonia synthesis for this reason.
answer: K is fixed. At fixed T, K = Ky (P/P°)Σν does not change; pressure and inerts change only the mole-fraction product Ky.
Pressure. Ky = K (P/P°)−Σν. For Σν < 0, −Σν > 0, so raising P raises the Ky the mixture must reach, pushing it toward products, the side with fewer gas moles.
Inerts. An inert adds to nT but not to K. At fixed P it lowers every yᵢ, which acts like a lower pressure on the reacting species; for Σν < 0 this shifts the equilibrium back toward reactants.
Ammonia at 500 K (K = 0.100), stoichiometric feed. With conversion X: K = 16X²(2 − X)²/[27(1 − X)⁴] × (P°/P)².
With inert. 0.444 mol Ar with 4 mol feed is 10 mol %; nT = 4.444 − 2X replaces 4 − 2X, the left side becomes 4X²(4.444 − 2X)²/[27(1 − X)⁴] and the solution falls from 0.846 to 0.832.

Industry. Synthesis loops run at high pressure for conversion, and a purge stream removes argon and methane that would otherwise build up and lower conversion. The purge loses some reactant, so the purge rate is a trade-off.

bank.q: A liquid-phase reaction A + B ⇌ C is run at 350 K with K = 4.00 and a feed of 1 mol A and 1 mol B. Show how K is converted to a composition relation, find the equilibrium extent for an ideal solution, and show how activity coefficients with K<sub>γ</sub> = γ<sub>C</sub>/(γ<sub>A</sub>γ<sub>B</sub>) = 0.80 change it.
outline: K = a<sub>C</sub>/(a<sub>A</sub> a<sub>B</sub>) with aᵢ = γᵢxᵢ.
So K = (γ<sub>C</sub>/γ<sub>A</sub>γ<sub>B</sub>)(x<sub>C</sub>/x<sub>A</sub> x<sub>B</sub>) = K<sub>γ</sub> K<sub>x</sub>.
Since liquids are incompressible, pressure has almost no effect on K; the standard state is the pure liquid at 1 bar.
K<sub>x</sub> = K/K<sub>γ</sub> requires γᵢ from a model (Margules, van Laar, NRTL, UNIFAC).
Solve K<sub>x</sub> with the mole balance xᵢ = (nᵢ₀ + νᵢξ)/n<sub>total</sub> for ξ.
Note dilute solutes need a Henry-based standard state instead.
answer: K in activities. K = aC/(aA aB) with aᵢ = γᵢxᵢ (pure-liquid standard states), so K = (γC/γAγB)(xC/xA xB) = Kγ Kx.
Mole balance. nA = nB = 1 − ξ, nC = ξ, nT = 2 − ξ; xA = xB = (1 − ξ)/(2 − ξ), xC = ξ/(2 − ξ). Then Kx = ξ(2 − ξ)/(1 − ξ)².
Ideal solution (Kγ = 1). ξ(2 − ξ)/(1 − ξ)² = 4.00. Let u = 1 − ξ: (1 − u²)/u² = 4, so u² = 0.2, u = 0.4472 and ξ = 0.553 mol. Composition: xA = xB = 0.447/1.447 = 0.309, xC = 0.382.
Non-ideal solution (Kγ = 0.80). Kx = K/Kγ = 4.00/0.80 = 5.00, so u² = 1/6, u = 0.4082 and ξ = 0.592 mol: the activity coefficients raise the conversion from 55.3 % to 59.2 %.

Real case. γᵢ depend on composition, so iterate: start with γᵢ = 1, solve for ξ, compute xᵢ, update γᵢ from a model (Margules, van Laar, Wilson, NRTL or UNIFAC), and repeat until ξ stops changing. Check by back-substitution that Π(γᵢxᵢ)νᵢ = K.
Pressure. Liquids are nearly incompressible; the Poynting-type change of K with pressure is tiny at ordinary pressures, so P is not a design lever for liquid-phase reactions.
Standard states. Pure liquid at T for each species. A dilute solute may need a Henry or molality standard state; then K must be the one tabulated for that choice.

bank.q: Carbon monoxide is shifted with steam: CO + H₂O ⇌ CO₂ + H₂, with a side reaction CO + 3H₂ ⇌ CH₄ + H₂O. Set up the multireaction equilibrium problem.
outline: Identify two independent reactions; check R = N − rank(A) with species CO, H₂O, CO₂, H₂, CH₄.
Introduce ξ₁ and ξ₂; write every nᵢ and total moles.
Write two equilibrium relations K₁ = Π aᵢ<sup>νᵢ</sup>¹ and K₂ = Π aᵢ<sup>νᵢ</sup>² at the same T.
Add carbon, hydrogen and oxygen balances; show only two are independent.
Solve the coupled nonlinear equations in ξ₁, ξ₂ numerically; compare with Gibbs minimisation.
Note Σν = 0 for the shift reaction, so pressure leaves that one unaffected.
answer: Species and reactions. CO, H₂O, CO₂, H₂ and CH₄ (N = 5) built from C, H and O. The atom matrix has rank 3, so R = 5 − 3 = 2 independent reactions: (1) CO + H₂O ⇌ CO₂ + H₂ and (2) CO + 3H₂ ⇌ CH₄ + H₂O.

answer.text: Mole numbers for a feed of 1 mol CO and 2 mol H₂O:
answer.pre:
CO  = 1 − ξ₁ − ξ₂
H₂O = 2 − ξ₁ + ξ₂
CO₂ = ξ₁
H₂  = ξ₁ − 3ξ₂
CH₄ = ξ₂
n<sub>T</sub> = 3 − 2ξ₂

answer: Equilibrium relations (ideal gas): K₁ = yCO₂yH₂/(yCOyH₂O), with Σν₁ = 0 so pressure cancels; K₂ = yCH₄yH₂O/(yCOyH₂³) × (P/P°)⁻², with Σν₂ = −2, so high pressure favours methane.

Element balances. C: nCO + nCO₂ + nCH₄ = 1; O: nCO + nH₂O + 2nCO₂ = 3; H: 2nH₂O + 2nH₂ + 4nCH₄ = 4. These hold automatically for any ξ₁, ξ₂; with five species and three independent balances, two extents remain, matching R = 2.

Solving. Two nonlinear equations in ξ₁ and ξ₂: use Newton's method from a start such as ξ₂ = 0 and ξ₁ from reaction (1) alone. With K₁ = 1.00 (near 1100 K) and methanation negligible, ξ₁ = 0.667 mol; any methane then forms by consuming H₂. Reject roots that make any nᵢ negative.
Check route. Gibbs minimisation over the five species with the three element balances gives the same answer without choosing the reactions.

Design reading. The shift is pressure-neutral and favoured by excess steam and lower T (exothermic); methanation is favoured by high pressure and low T, so a shift reactor runs at moderate pressure with excess steam to keep CH₄ low.

bank.q: A gas mixture of 20 mol % NH₃, 20 mol % N₂ and 60 mol % H₂ is held at 500 K and 100 bar, where K = 0.100 for N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃. Explain how you decide whether the forward reaction, the reverse reaction or nothing happens, and apply it.
outline: Compute the reaction quotient Q = Π aᵢ<sup>νᵢ</sup> from the actual composition.
Compare Q with K: Q < K forward feasible, Q > K reverse feasible, Q = K at equilibrium.
Relate the sign of ΔG = RT ln(Q/K) to the direction; negative ΔG means the forward direction is spontaneous.
State that K depends only on T, so temperature decides how far the system can go while Q sets the starting point.
Mention that a large negative ΔG° does not fix the conversion — thermodynamics and kinetics are separate questions.
answer: Reaction quotient. Q = Π aᵢνᵢ evaluated at the actual composition; for ideal gases aᵢ = yᵢP/P°.
Test. ΔG = ΔG° + RT ln Q = RT ln(Q/K). Q < K: ΔG < 0, forward. Q > K: ΔG > 0, reverse. Q = K: equilibrium, nothing happens.

Conclusion. Q is about a thousand times smaller than K, so ΔG = −29.0 kJ per mole of reaction and the forward reaction (more ammonia) is spontaneous. The mixture would move toward the equilibrium of the previous answers, with yNH₃ near 0.7 at this T and P.
K versus Q. K depends only on T and sets where the mixture can end; Q depends on the present composition and pressure and sets the starting point. Changing P changes Q (through (P/P°)Σν) but not K.

Thermodynamics is not kinetics. A negative ΔG says the reaction can go, not how fast. At 500 K ammonia synthesis is very slow even on a catalyst, which is why plants accept a lower K at 650–750 K to get a usable rate.

bank.q: Discuss the choice between K<sub>p</sub>, K<sub>y</sub> and K<sub>a</sub> for gas-phase equilibria, and assess when fugacity coefficients can be ignored.
outline: Define f̂ᵢ = yᵢφᵢP and K = Π (f̂ᵢ/fᵢ°)<sup>νᵢ</sup>.
At low pressure φᵢ → 1 so K ≈ K<sub>p</sub> = Π (yᵢP/P°)<sup>νᵢ</sup>.
Write K = K<sub>y</sub> K<sub>φ</sub> (P/P°)<sup>Σν</sup> to separate composition, nonideality and pressure.
Judging rule: ignore φᵢ near 1 bar; at 100 bar and above use an equation of state or generalised charts.
Example: ammonia synthesis at 200–300 bar has φᵢ far from unity.
Conclusion: K<sub>a</sub> is the rigorous constant; K<sub>p</sub> and K<sub>y</sub> are approximations valid in stated limits.
answer: Rigorous constant. K = Π(f̂ᵢ/fᵢ°)νᵢ with f̂ᵢ = φ̂ᵢyᵢP and fᵢ° = P° = 1 bar for every gas. This is Ka, the activity-based constant fixed by ΔG°.
Splitting it. K = Ky Kφ (P/P°)Σν, where Ky = Πyᵢνᵢ carries the composition, Kφ = Πφ̂ᵢνᵢ the non-ideality and (P/P°)Σν the pressure.
Kp. Kp = Π(yᵢP)νᵢ in pressure units equals Ky PΣν; it equals K numerically only for ideal gases with pressures in bar (P° = 1 bar). It is convenient at low pressure.
Ky. Not a constant: at fixed T it changes with P (unless Σν = 0) and with non-ideality. It is the quantity actually solved for once K, P and Kφ are known.

When φ can be ignored. Near 1 bar and for gases well above their critical temperatures at moderate pressure, φ̂ᵢ ≈ 1 and Kφ ≈ 1. At 100 bar and above, or near the dew point, compute φ̂ᵢ from a virial or cubic equation of state.

Example. Ammonia at 500 K and 100 bar: the ideal-gas answer is 84.6 % conversion. At these conditions NH₃ has φ well below 1 while H₂ is slightly above 1, so Kφ < 1 and Ky = K/[Kφ(P/P°)Σν] is larger: the real conversion is somewhat higher than the ideal estimate. Ignoring Kφ in a 200–300 bar loop gives a noticeable error.
Conclusion. Use K (Ka) as the defining constant; treat Kp as its low-pressure form and Ky as the derived composition product.

bank.q: For a heterogeneous reaction such as CaCO₃(s) ⇌ CaO(s) + CO₂(g), derive the equilibrium relation and explain why solids drop out of K.
outline: Write K = a<sub>CO₂</sub> a<sub>CaO</sub> / a<sub>CaCO₃</sub> with each pure solid at unit activity.
A pure solid at the system T and P is in its standard state (pressure effect negligible), so its activity is 1 and K = a<sub>CO₂</sub> = f̂<sub>C</sub>O₂/P° ≈ p<sub>CO₂</sub>/P°.
Hence the decomposition pressure is fixed by T alone, giving K = p<sub>CO₂</sub>/P° and p<sub>CO₂</sub> = K P°.
Show that adding or removing solid changes nothing at equilibrium as long as both phases persist.
Distinguish cases where a solid is consumed completely, where the activity term no longer applies.
Link to calcination temperature in lime kilns and to the phase rule for reacting systems.
answer: Equilibrium relation. CaCO₃(s) ⇌ CaO(s) + CO₂(g): K = aCaO aCO₂/aCaCO₃.

Why solids drop out. Each solid is a separate pure phase. Its standard state is the pure solid at T (and 1 bar); at the system pressure its chemical potential differs from μ° only by ∫V dP, which is negligible for a solid, so a = 1 whatever the amount. Hence K = aCO₂ = f̂CO₂/P° ≈ pCO₂/P°.
Decomposition pressure. At each T, pCO₂ = KP° is fixed: the equilibrium CO₂ pressure over limestone. If the surrounding CO₂ pressure is below it, the solid decomposes; above it, CaO takes up CO₂.

Amounts do not matter. Adding more CaCO₃ or CaO changes nothing as long as both solids are present, because neither appears in K. If one solid is used up, it is no longer a phase and the relation K = pCO₂/P° no longer applies; pCO₂ is then set by the material balance.
Phase rule. N = 3 species, π = 3 phases, r = 1: F = 3 − 3 + 2 − 1 = 1. T alone fixes pCO₂, like a vapour-pressure curve.

From data. ln K = −ΔG°/RT with ΔG° = ΔGf°(CaO) + ΔGf°(CO₂) − ΔGf°(CaCO₃) at T. The decomposition is strongly endothermic (ΔH° about +178 kJ/mol), so K rises steeply with T; pCO₂ reaches 1 bar at roughly 1170 K, which is why lime kilns run near 900 °C or above and sweep CO₂ away.
Other examples. C(s) + CO₂ ⇌ 2CO: K = (yCOP/P°)²/(yCO₂P/P°); metal oxide reduction by H₂ or CO is handled the same way.

bank.q: Compare the two routes to multireaction equilibrium — solving R equations Σνᵢⱼμᵢ = 0 with element balances, and direct Gibbs energy minimisation — and assess their merits.
outline: Route 1: choose R independent reactions, write R equilibrium constants plus element balances, solve for R extents.
Route 2: minimise G = Σnᵢμᵢ(nᵢ) subject to element balances, using Lagrange multipliers.
Show both use the same μᵢ model and give the same answer.
Advantage of minimisation: no need to guess a reaction set; danger of local minima and numerical stiffness.
Advantage of K-equations: physically transparent, easier to start, but needs known independent reactions.
Mention extent bounds nᵢ ≥ 0 and that nonnegativity constraints matter in practical solvers.
answer: Route 1: reaction equations. Choose R = N − rank(A) independent reactions, write nᵢ = nᵢ₀ + Σνᵢⱼξⱼ, and solve the R equations Kⱼ = Π aᵢνᵢⱼ for the R extents. The element balances are satisfied automatically.

Route 2: Gibbs minimisation. Minimise G = Σnᵢμᵢ(T, P, n) over all nᵢ ≥ 0 subject to the element balances Σnᵢaik = Ak. With Lagrange multipliers λk: μᵢ + Σk λk aik = 0 for each species, i.e. μᵢ/RT = ΔGf,i°/RT + ln(yᵢP/P°) = −Σλk aik/RT for ideal gases.
Same answer. Both use the same μᵢ model and the same conservation laws; at the solution of route 2, Σνᵢⱼμᵢ = 0 holds for any reaction vector, which is route 1.

head: Aspect
K-equations
Gibbs minimisation
rows: missing a reaction, negative nᵢ roots

answer: Example. For A ⇌ B (K₁ = 2.00) and 2A ⇌ C (K₂ = 0.500) at 1 bar from 1 mol A, route 1 gives ξ₁ = 0.603, ξ₂ = 0.0477 and yA = 0.317, yB = 0.633, yC = 0.050; minimising G over A, B and C with one balance on A-units gives the same.
Practice. Hand calculations and small systems use route 1; reactor simulators (Gibbs reactors) use route 2 with bounds nᵢ ≥ 0, which avoids guessing reactions and handles solids and phase splits.

bank.q: Assess how temperature, pressure and inert level together set the equilibrium conversion in an industrial gas reaction with Σν < 0 and ΔH° < 0.
outline: ΔH° < 0 means K falls as T rises, so low T favours conversion but slows kinetics.
Σν < 0 means high P favours conversion through K<sub>y</sub> = K(P/P°)<sup>−Σν</sup>.
Inerts dilute the mixture and cut conversion, so a purge stream is needed.
Optimal design therefore compromises with a moderate T, high P and low inert level.
Write the general K = K<sub>y</sub> K<sub>φ</sub> (P/P°)<sup>Σν</sup> relation and show each lever's role.
Note that reaction kinetics, catalyst life and compression cost set the practical limits.
answer: Temperature. ΔH° < 0, so K falls as T rises (van't Hoff). For ammonia synthesis K drops from 5.81 × 10⁵ at 298 K to 0.100 at 500 K and 8.56 × 10⁻⁵ at 700 K. Low T favours conversion, but rates are too slow there, so a catalyst and a compromise temperature (about 650–750 K) are used.
Pressure. Σν < 0, so Ky = K(P/P°)−Σν rises with P. At 500 K a stoichiometric feed converts 15.8 % of the N₂ at 1 bar but 84.6 % at 100 bar; at 700 K, 200 bar still gives 45.8 %.

Inerts. They dilute the reactants and lower conversion for Σν < 0: 10 mol % argon at 500 K and 100 bar lowers the conversion from 84.6 % to 83.2 %. In a recycle loop inerts accumulate, so a purge is needed.
All levers together. K = Ky Kφ (P/P°)Σν: T sets K; P enters through (P/P°)Σν; inerts change Ky through nT; non-ideality enters through Kφ.

Design. The result is a moderate temperature with a good catalyst, high pressure, product removal by condensation and recycle, and a controlled purge; kinetics, catalyst life and compression cost set the final choice.

bank.q: State the phase rule and Duhem's theorem for reacting systems and explain what they allow you to fix when designing an equilibrium calculation.
outline: Degrees of freedom F = N − π + 2 − r for N species, π phases and r independent reactions.
Explain why each independent reaction removes one degree of freedom: it adds a relation Σνᵢμᵢ = 0.
Duhem's theorem: for a closed system made from given amounts, fixing two independent variables fixes the whole equilibrium state, reacting or not; when F = 1 one must be extensive.
Consequence: composition at equilibrium follows from T and P plus feed and element balances.
Example: CaCO₃(s) ⇌ CaO(s) + CO₂(g) has N = 3, π = 3, r = 1, so F = 1: T alone fixes the CO₂ pressure, and the amounts of the solids need an extensive specification.
answer: Reacting phase rule. F = N − π + 2 − r, with N chemical species, π phases and r independent reactions (plus any special constraint s, subtracted the same way).

Why each reaction removes one freedom. The non-reacting count is F = N − π + 2. Each independent reaction adds one equation, Σνᵢⱼμᵢ = 0, among the same intensive variables, so it removes one degree of freedom.

Duhem's theorem. For a closed system made from given amounts of species, the equilibrium state, intensive and extensive, is fixed by any two independent variables, whether or not reactions occur. When F ≥ 2 both may be intensive (T and P); when F = 1 one must be extensive.

Reading F. For ammonia gas, F = 3: T, P and one composition variable, such as the N₂:H₂ ratio fixed by the feed. For steam reforming, T, P and two element ratios (for example C:H and O:H in the feed). For calcination, T alone fixes pCO₂.

Design use. A single-phase reactor fed a known mixture: fixing T and P fixes the equilibrium composition (Duhem), which is how the K calculations are posed. For the three-phase calcination, T fixes pCO₂, and the extent of decomposition needs an extensive specification such as the amount of CO₂ removed.

glossary.def: A single variable ξ in mol that measures how far a reaction has run; every mole number follows from nᵢ = nᵢ₀ + νᵢξ.
The fixed molar ratios in which species appear in a balanced chemical equation.
The reactant that runs out first and therefore caps the maximum possible conversion.
The state in which no further net change of composition occurs at fixed temperature and pressure.
The partial molar Gibbs energy of a species, equal to the change in G when one mole is added at fixed T, P and other amounts.
A = −Σνᵢμᵢ in J/mol; positive when the forward reaction is spontaneous, zero at equilibrium.
The numerical method of finding equilibrium composition by minimising total G subject to element balances.
The agreed reference state, at unit activity, against which Gibbs energies and activities are measured.
The dimensionless effective amount of a species relative to its standard state; equals 1 for a pure liquid or solid at 1 bar.
An effective pressure that makes the ideal-gas chemical potential formula work for real gases.
The temperature-dependent number K = Π aᵢ<sup>νᵢ</sup> evaluated at equilibrium; related to ΔG° by ΔG° = −RT ln K.
ΔG°f of a compound: the change in Gibbs energy when one mole forms from elements in their standard states.
A reaction with ΔH° > 0; its equilibrium constant rises as temperature rises.
A reaction with ΔH° < 0; its equilibrium constant falls as temperature rises.
Q = Π aᵢ<sup>νᵢ</sup> at the actual composition; comparison with K tells the direction of change.
The fraction of the fed limiting reactant that has reacted when equilibrium is reached.
The fraction of reacted feed that ends up as the desired product rather than a by-product.
The equilibrium constant expressed in partial pressures, K<sub>p</sub> = Π(pᵢ/p°)<sup>νᵢ</sup>, valid for ideal gases.
The equilibrium constant expressed in mole fractions, K<sub>y</sub> = Π yᵢ<sup>νᵢ</sup>; carries all the composition dependence for gases.
A species present in the mixture that takes no part in the reaction but adds to the total moles.
A minimal set of reactions whose extents can describe every possible composition change of the system.
A reaction involving more than one phase, so each pure condensed phase contributes unit activity.
Fixing any two independent intensive properties of a closed system fixes all its remaining intensive properties.
F = N − π + 2 − r, where C counts components, P counts phases and R counts independent reactions.
